props.title: There Will Be Blood
props.initialSlug: Oil tycoon's ruthless pursuit of wealth consumes his soul

sections.content: There Will Be Blood (2007) stands as Paul Thomas Anderson's masterpiece of American capitalism and spiritual corruption. Daniel Day-Lewis delivers a towering performance as Daniel Plainview, a performance that draws from classic frontier films like The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (1948) while creating something entirely new. The film's opening 15 minutes, nearly dialogue-free, recall the wordless sequences of 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), showing Plainview's relentless drive through pure visual storytelling. Anderson's collaboration with cinematographer Robert Elswit produces stark, haunting images of California oil fields that echo the work of still photographer Edward Curtis.

sections.content: The film's exploration of the intersection between capitalism and religion builds on themes from classics like Elmer Gantry (1960) but pushes into darker territory. Paul Dano's performance as twin brothers Paul and Eli Sunday creates an unsettling mirror to Plainview's corruption, suggesting that religious fervor and capitalist greed are two sides of the same coin. The score by Jonny Greenwood breaks radically from traditional period film music, using dissonant orchestral techniques reminiscent of The Shining (1980) to create a sense of mounting dread.

The film's visual style draws heavily from the American western tradition while subverting it. Like McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971), it strips away romantic myths about frontier entrepreneurship. Anderson's long takes and precise compositions recall Barry Lyndon (1975), another story about a ruthless social climber, but with a distinctly American darkness. The famous "I drink your milkshake" finale, while often quoted, serves as a devastating culmination of themes about consumption, competition, and spiritual emptiness. SUBHEAD: Oil, Power, and the American Dream

sections.content: Anderson's film belongs to a tradition of American movies about oil and power, including Giant (1956) and The Day of the Oil (1979), but none match its intensity. The film's attention to period detail in depicting early 20th century oil extraction techniques grounds its larger metaphysical themes in concrete historical reality. Like Chinatown (1974), it shows how California's resources were exploited by ruthless men, though Anderson pushes beyond historical critique into psychological horror.
